findings.evidence: "The finance office reviews overdue notice counts on the first of every month. Historical figures are archived for five years before being summarized and retired."
findings.fix: Remove this paragraph or replace it with actual circulation trend data relevant to the fines decision.
findings.violation: This paragraph is filed under "Circulation Trends" but contains no circulation data or trend - only an administrative review/retention schedule - and has no bearing on the fines recommendation.

findings.evidence: "The finance office reviews self-checkout usage at the end of each quarter. Branch-level totals roll up into the consortium's shared reporting dashboard."
findings.fix: Delete this paragraph or explain its relevance to the fines decision if one exists.
findings.violation: Self-checkout usage and dashboard reporting cadence are unrelated to overdue fines or circulation trends and contribute nothing to the argument.

findings.evidence: "the on-time-or-eventual return rate for borrowed items held at 93 percent"
findings.fix: Report on-time return rate and eventual (late) return rate as separate figures so the effect of removing fines on lateness can be evaluated.
findings.violation: Combining "on-time" and "eventual" returns into one statistic hides whether eliminating fines increased late-but-still-returned items, which is the behavior most relevant to assessing the policy's effect.

findings.evidence: "93 percent, compared with 86 percent at the branches that kept fines in place"
findings.fix: Include sample sizes and a significance test (or confidence interval) for the comparison.
findings.violation: No sample size, number of items/patrons, or statistical significance is given, so it's impossible to judge whether the 7-point gap is a meaningful effect or noise.

findings.evidence: "The survey was administered at the same pilot branches immediately before and twelve months into the pilot."
findings.fix: Either administer the survey at the pilot's actual conclusion (18 months) or explain why the 12-month mark was chosen and what, if anything, changed afterward.
findings.violation: The pilot ran 18 months, but the survey's second measurement was taken at 12 months, leaving the final 6 months of the pilot unassessed by the survey.

findings.evidence: "the stronger choice is a systemwide end to overdue fines across all ten consortium branches"
findings.fix: Either qualify the recommendation as applying first to branches comparable to the pilot sites, or note the extrapolation as an assumption requiring further validation.
findings.violation: The pilot tested only 5 of the 10 branches; the recommendation extrapolates the result to the other 5 branches without evidence they would behave similarly.

findings.evidence: "replacing the current fine notices with automatic email reminders sent three, seven, and fourteen days after the due date"
findings.fix: State explicitly what intervention the pilot branches used in place of fines, and confirm the proposed 3/7/14-day email schedule matches it, or label it as an untested new element.
findings.violation: This specific reminder schedule is presented as part of the recommended change, but nothing in the pilot description indicates this schedule (or any email reminder system) was what was actually tested at the pilot branches.

findings.evidence: "matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established"
findings.fix: Either present the pilot data on return-time distribution that supports the 60-day cutoff, or remove the claim that it matches an established pattern.
findings.violation: No data about a 60-day return window, or any breakdown of how long it took items to be returned, appears anywhere in the "What the Pilot Showed" section, so this claim of a matching pattern is unsupported by the evidence presented.

findings.evidence: "The systems team plans to update the online catalog's fine-display field during the same rollout window."
findings.fix: Remove this sentence or move it to an implementation/logistics section, and replace it with actual evidence or reasoning for systemwide applicability.
findings.location: "Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide" section, first line
findings.violation: This sentence is an unrelated implementation detail about the catalog system and provides no argument for why the pilot result generalizes systemwide, despite the section heading.

findings.evidence: "This is simply how patron behavior works, and no library that has tried it has ever found otherwise."
findings.fix: Remove the claim or replace it with specific evidence (e.g., comparable outcomes reported by other library systems, with citations) supporting generalizability.
findings.location: "Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide" section, second line
findings.violation: This is an unsupported, sweeping universal claim with no citation or evidence, which undermines the document's otherwise data-driven framing and does not actually justify systemwide generalization from a 5-branch pilot.

findings.evidence: "argues that eliminating them systemwide will leave a shortfall the consortium has not planned for" followed only by "The branch renovation project remains on schedule for completion next spring."
findings.fix: Provide a substantive response to the revenue concern - e.g., projected fine revenue lost, alternative funding sources, or data from the pilot on materials-replacement costs - or remove the section heading's implied promise.
findings.violation: The section heading promises to address the revenue/funding-shortfall concern, but the only content provided is an unrelated fact about a renovation project; the revenue concern is never actually answered.
